ety.text: From Middle English today, to-daie, todæig, from Old English tōdæġ, tō dæġe (“today”, literally “on [the/this] day, [this] day forward”), equivalent to to + day. Compare Saterland Frisian däälich (“today”), Dutch vandaag (“today”), Old Saxon hindag (“today”, literally “[this] day forward”), German Low German vandage, vandaag (“today”), Swedish i dag, idag (“today”).

senses.d: On the current day or date.
ex: Today, my brother went to the shops.

senses.d: In the current era; nowadays; these days.
ex: In the 1500s, people had to do things by hand, but today we have electric can openers.

senses.d: On the day of a recurring cycle or event which is currently happening.
ex: We used to prepare everything today, but now we split it over two days.
Today is the day we'll fix this once and for all.
We could've spent today at the seaside if it weren't gusty.

senses.d: The 24-hour period beginning at 5 or 6 a.m. or sunrise of the current day.

ex: This is the sporty jacket for today's modern man on the go.
The youth of today have never known what life is like without a cell phone.
Actually, it's more like the blues. It's pop blues. I feel it's very American. It's very today. It's what people respond to today.

grp.label: nowadays — see also nowadays, these days, currently

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French auiourd'huy; univerbation of au + jour + de + hui, literally “on the day of today”; since hui comes from Latin hodie.
Inherited from Old Spanish oy, from Latin hodiē. Cognate with Portuguese hoje, and Italian oggi.

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese oge (“today”), from Latin hodiē (“today”), from hōc (“this”) + diē (“day”). Cognate with Galician hoxe, Spanish hoy, Catalan avui, French hui and Italian oggi.

ety.text: From toddle (“to walk unsteadily”) + -er – literally “one who walks unsteadily”, hence a young child.

senses.d: A young child (typically between one and three years old) who has started walking but not fully mastered it.
ex: I can't believe Vanessa's baby is now a toddler already!

senses.d: Any young child (typically before preadolescence) who is capable of walking.
ex: He gave up, said the sixes were being too rowdy... Can't believe he's scared of literal toddlers!

grp.label: young child who has started walking but not fully mastered it

ety.text: Borrowed from Italian bambino, from onomatopoeic bambo for the first stammerings of children.

Nickname given to Nicolas Ferry, renowned throughout Europe as the court dwarf of the Polish King Stanisław Leszczyński. Possibly derived from bab- (babiller, babine) rather than adapted from English baby, although this may have contributed to the diffusion of the word.

it:bambino.gl: child, baby, toddler, tot (male or of unspecified gender)

ety.text: Onomatopoeic bambo for the first stammerings of children, plus -ino (diminutive suffix).

Uncertain. Possibly from: * An onomatopoeic root or children's/nursery word *pikk-, *picc-. * From Vulgar Latin *pikk (“little”), related to *piccāre (“to pierce”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (“to make a dull, hollow sound”). * From picca (“point”).
